one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban observes that high-profile criminal cases normally begin in the regional trial courts or in the Sandiganbayan, where the presiding magistrates bear the brunt of public scrutiny -- praised or damned by the peanut gallery -- and where the sub judice rule is relaxed in favor of fair comment and free speech, so that 'trial judges are put on trial in the courts of public opinion.' He uses the three drug-trafficking cases filed against former Senator Leila de Lima (and several others), raffled to three branches of the Regional Trial Courts of Muntinlupa, as his case studies. In one case she was acquitted 'without much ado.' In another, Branch 204 (Presiding Judge Abraham Joseph Alcantara) acquitted her on the ground that -- though the crime may have been committed -- the recantation of former NBI Director Rafael Ragos created doubt on her participation. In the third, Branch 256 (Presiding Judge Romeo Buenaventura) denied her motion for bail because the prosecution's evidence was 'strong.' He cross-references his four earlier columns on the De Lima cases (Jan 30, June 5, June 12, June 26) and pivots here to the judges' tribulations. Judge Alcantara's acquittal -- normally final and unappealable -- is now under attack via a formidable 71-page OSG petition for certiorari in the Court of Appeals seeking to declare it null and void for 'grave abuse of discretion,' under which a decision so found is deemed nonexistent and the acquittal would be void; while certiorari petitions ordinarily face the strong presumption of judicial diligence, the SolGen Menardo I. Guevarra's reputation for probity and fairness strengthens this one, exposing Alcantara's competence and honesty to adverse findings and potential administrative liability -- even though he is not required to defend the decision himself (that burden falls on the accused and her lawyers). Judge Buenaventura, separately, faces a personal administrative complaint before the Judicial Integrity Board (JIB) -- not over the bail-denial order (subject to a separate attack) but for inhibiting only after a motion to inhibit had been filed showing that his brother Erwin had prepared an affidavit of one of the accused. The complaint by De Lima's counsels in the JIB charges him with not immediately disclosing his prohibited relationship, unreasonably delaying the case and forcing a new raffle to Branch 206 under Judge Gener Gito, who understandably needs time to study the case anew -- prolonging the accused's detention. Because the complaint is personal, Judge Buenaventura must retain and pay for his own counsel. He credentializes the JIB -- created a few years ago by the SC to investigate misbehaving magistrates and judicial personnel nationwide, headed by retired Justices Romeo J. Callejo Sr. (chair) and Angelina Sandoval-Gutierrez (vice chair) -- as 'quietly chasing shenanigans in the judiciary.' He closes by categorizing trial-judge risks and tribulations: 'some self-inflicted, some by failure to follow the ethical codes, some by neglect to live up to the constitutional standards of proven competence, integrity, probity, and independence, and some by conveniently ignoring what I call the plague of ships: kinship, relationship, friendship, and fellowship.'
